newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Waigel relieved as his budget pact sails through.
newsitem.headline: Waigel relieved as his budget pact sails through.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the architect of the stability pact aimed at ensuring fiscal discipline within a European currency, glowed with quiet triumph as his pet project was finally adopted on Monday.

Clearly relieved that the new French left-wing government had backed off on its threats to refuse to sign up to the deal, Waigel made clear that the last-minute quibbling about the pact had done nothing to weaken the final pact agreed. "The pact was adopted without any change -- not a comma, not a full stop was altered," he said following a meeting with other finance ministers on the fringes of a summit meeting in the Dutch capital of Amsterdam.

France instead won a series of commitments that the European Union would work together to combat unemployment, anchored in a resolution presented to the summit meeting of EU leaders by their finance ministers.

Waigel himself painted the resolution on employment and growth -- approved by the summit in a bid to appease the French -- in a positive light, making clear Bonn's worst fears had not been realised as there were no commitments for new spending.
Reporting to journalists after the ministers' meeting, he said: "The employment resolution is so arranged that no additional financial resources are involved."

Waigel also supported plans for a special employment summit, expected to take place in the autumn, to look into what the European Union can do to cut its jobless queues. "Nobody can have anything against a jobs summit," he said.
On the jobs and growth resolution, he said, "We can live happily with that, including the resolution on growth and jobs, because it involves no extra resources."

Germany and France were plunged into an unusually high-profile dispute when the new French government, led by socialist Lionel Jospin, announced it needed more time to study the stability pact and could not agree it, as planned, in Amsterdam.
Only frantic negotiation over the last week brought the 15-member group to a compromise position.

Asked at a news conference after the first day of summit talks whether he would rank the stabilty pact at the same level as the hastily-assembled growth and stability pact, Waigel made clear that France's scramble for recognition of the region's employment problems was less than ideal.

"One of the two was discussed for one-and-a-half years and will now become part of secondary legislation," he said. "On the other hand we have something which we have worked on intensively for the last week, but which is nonetheless of great importance.
"This underscores the necessity for the stability pact. If we went away from that then the unemployment plan would have no chance," he added.

A strong stability pact has become one of the Bonn government's best selling points for the unpopular single currency, with public finances in most European nations looking less than healthy as the euro launch date creeps closer.

Germany, which once set an example to Europe with a balanced budget, is itself perilously close to overshooting a deficit goal of three percent of gross domestic product this year, the key year for decisions on entry to monetary union.

Reflecting Germany's domestic budget problems, Waigel formally announced in Amsterdam that he would not be joining German Chancellor Helmut Kohl at a meeting of the world's seven richest nations in Denver, Colorado, this week.
Confirming an announcement made in Bonn in his absence, Waigel said, "It seems more important (to stay at home) than to take part in the also important event in Denver."
